title: How the Escape from Alcatraz Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the 1962 escape from Alcatraz by Frank Morris and the English brothers (J.W. and Clarence), with Alan West left behind. They cover the criminal backgrounds of the escapees, Alcatraz's reputation as inescapable, the months-long plan (paper-mache dummy heads, cell wall holes, raincoat life raft, tools made from stolen prison items), the night of June 11, 1962, the aftermath and FBI/Marshals investigation, the bodies-sighting and Seymour Webb evidence, the 2013 letter and Brazil photo claims, and theories about survival. The episode opens with book pre-order promotion and banter, includes an ad break, and closes with a pitch for the book and a listener mail segment about Delaware. Also mentions the 1979 Clint Eastwood film Escape from Alcatraz and that the film departs from the facts.

segments.title: Book pre-order plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts plug their upcoming book Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things, then chat about Gene Wilder, Conan O'Brien, Ken Jennings, and Chuck's squirrel attack story before turning to the episode topic.

segments.title: Who the escapees were
segments.summary: Introduces Frank Morris, the English brothers J.W. and Clarence, and their criminal backgrounds. Morris had a high IQ reportedly in the top two percent of the prison system. The Englands robbed a bank in Columbia, Alabama with a toy gun and got 25-year sentences. The hosts discuss how the 1979 Clint Eastwood film compares with the facts, and how the escapees became folk heroes.

segments.title: Alcatraz as an inescapable prison
segments.summary: Describes Alcatraz's cold, strong-current bay, the prison's history from Army use, the Bureau of Prisons fortifying the cell blocks, and the earlier escape attempts, including Ted Cole and Ralph Roe who vanished in the late 1930s. Morris and the Englands were sent there after meeting at the Atlanta federal penitentiary.

segments.title: Tools and the escape plan preparation
segments.summary: The men spent about six months gathering and making tools. Alan West, a painter on the prison crew, stole electric clippers from the barbershop and used a vacuum motor to build a powerful drill. The group obtained rubber raincoats from other inmates. They worked three and a half hours each evening after dinner.

segments.title: Digging out of the cells and the ventilation shaft
segments.summary: The men enlarged ventilation grates in their cells by chipping at the cement, taking turns as lookouts. They used cardboard or paper-mache false walls and dummy heads with prison hair to fool guards. They reached a utility corridor, built a workshop there, and then worked on the ventilation shaft's iron grate by loosening its bolts.

segments.title: The life raft and the night of the escape
segments.summary: The raft was built from raincoats, inflated with a modified concertina, and sealed by vulcanizing seams, an idea taken from a Popular Mechanics article. Alan West had the raft job and fell behind. On the night of Monday June 11, the three men left their cells and went to the roof and then down a drain pipe to the perimeter fence. West was left behind and was pinned by a guard until dawn, and then returned to his cell.

segments.title: Alan West's account and the planned route
segments.summary: Almost everything known comes from Alan West's statements to the Bureau of Prisons and FBI, given in exchange for immunity. The planned route was to paddle to Angel Island, then swim to Marin County via Raccoon Straits, then steal clothes, money and a car. Search efforts found a life preserver, a wallet and an oar, but no bodies.

segments.title: Sightings, Seymour Webb, Brazil letter and survival theories
segments.summary: The FBI cited Seymour Webb, who jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge at about the same time, as a comparison. A body in jeans was seen by Norwegian sailors in July 1962. Brazil photo analysis and a 2013 letter to SFPD claimed survival. The US Marshals kept the case open. The hosts discuss the weather and tides, the cold water, and the Alcatraz closure in March 1963.

segments.title: Listener mail: Delaware response
segments.summary: A listener from Delaware, Doug Wazgat, responds to earlier jokes about Delaware, describing the state's history, its arc-shaped border from a twelve-mile radius around Newcastle, and the disputed wedge of land.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts repeat the book plug and invite listener mail, then sign off.
